examples.solution_text:
Take out the common factor $3$ first.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}12x^2-75\\&=3(4x^2-25)\\&=3\big((2x)^2-5^2\big)\\&=3(2x-5)(2x+5)\end{aligned}$
Both brackets have no further common factor.

The first and last terms are $(4x)^2$ and $(5y)^2$. Check the middle term: $-2(4x)(5y)=-40xy$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}16x^2-40xy+25y^2\\&=(4x)^2-2(4x)(5y)+(5y)^2\\&=(4x-5y)^2\end{aligned}$

Take out the common factor $5$. Inside the brackets, $2(x)(3)=6x$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}5x^2+30x+45\\&=5(x^2+6x+9)\\&=5\big(x^2+2(x)(3)+3^2\big)\\&=5(x+3)^2\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Can $x^2+16$ be factorised using the difference of two squares? Explain.
examples.solution_text: $x^2+16=x^2+4^2$. The squares are added, so the difference of two squares rule does not apply. This expression has no real linear factors.

Apply the difference of two squares twice.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}x^4-625\\&=(x^2)^2-25^2\\&=(x^2-25)(x^2+25)\\&=(x-5)(x+5)(x^2+25)\end{aligned}$
The sum of squares $x^2+25$ has no real linear factors.

Factorise each pair, using a negative factor for the second pair so the brackets match.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}12xy+8x-9y-6\\&=(12xy+8x)+(-9y-6)\\&=4x(3y+2)-3(3y+2)\\&=(3y+2)(4x-3)\end{aligned}$

examples.solution_text:
Treat the whole bracket $(x-2)$ as the second squared term. Keep its brackets when subtracting.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}36-(x-2)^2\\&=6^2-(x-2)^2\\&=\big(6-(x-2)\big)\big(6+(x-2)\big)\\&=(8-x)(x+4)\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: The HCF is 3: 12x²−75=3(4x²−25)=3(2x−5)(2x+5). Both linear brackets have coprime integer coefficients.
5x²+30x+45=5(x²+6x+9). Since 6x=2(x)(3), the fully factorised answer is 5(x+3)².
x²+16 is a sum of squares. It is positive for every real x, so it has no real roots and no real linear factors; the difference rule does not apply.
625=25², so x⁴−625=(x²−25)(x²+25)=(x−5)(x+5)(x²+25). The remaining sum of squares has no real linear factors.
12xy+8x=4x(3y+2) and −9y−6=−3(3y+2). Taking out the matching binomial gives (3y+2)(4x−3), whose expansion restores all four terms.
